clue.text: Foreign labourer's reported in a less than friendly way

definitions.text: in a less than friendly way

indicators.note: reported means passed on by word of mouth, so we want what a word sounds like when spoken

parts.note: a coolie is a dated term for an unskilled labourer from Asia; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A migrant worker is said to have been treated with some frostiness.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting with chilly reserve is behaving in an unfriendly manner, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Pause, about to turn a trick

parts.note: CA is short for circa, about

indicators.note: to turn means to swing round, so the following pieces read backwards

parts.note: a ruse is a trick

explanation.surface: A magician pauses before turning a card trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to turn' reverses A RUSE into ESURA.
explanation.definitionFit: A caesura is a break or rest in a line of verse or music.

clue.text: Remaining to be gagged by Rothermere

indicators.note: gagged suggests being held inside a mouth, so the letters sit inside the name

explanation.surface: Someone still left is to be silenced by the press baron Rothermere.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Rothermere owns the Daily Mail.
explanation.definitionFit: Other as in 'the other ones' means the rest, those remaining.

clue.text: US city's less than clean

parts.note: LA is Los Angeles
under means less than, as in under ten

explanation.surface: An American city is said to be rather dirty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'less than clean' looks like one phrase but splits.
explanation.definitionFit: To launder is to wash clothes, or to clean dirty money.

clue.text: Article penned by Dacre's 80% wild, unfounded rumour

indicators.note: something penned by another is enclosed by it, as if in a pen
wild suggests letters running out of control into a new order
eighty per cent of a five-letter name keeps four letters, dropping the last

parts.note: Paul Dacre, former editor of the Daily Mail
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper story written by the Mail's editor is mostly baseless gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: '80%' keeps four of the five letters of the editor's name, DACR; 'wild' makes CARD of them. Paul Dacre edited the Daily Mail.
explanation.definitionFit: A canard is a false story or hoax spread about, i.e. a baseless rumour.

clue.text: Jobs creation long moved south following a request

indicators.note: in a down entry, moving south means shifting lower in the word

parts.note: Steve Jobs co-founded the Apple computer company

explanation.surface: A job-creation scheme moved south after a plea.
explanation.walkthrough: The L of APPLE moves down to sit after the A.
explanation.definitionFit: An appeal is a plea or earnest request.

clue.text: Reverse order

definitions.meaning: a complete change of direction or policy
a drill command telling soldiers to face the other way

explanation.surface: A command given in the reverse direction.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a U-turn in policy and the parade-ground command to face backwards.

clue.text: Chaperones Miss Widdecombe in retirement, charging fees

indicators.note: charging in the sense of loading, so fees carry the name within

parts.note: dues are fees

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the name is read backwards

parts.note: Ann Widdecombe is a former Conservative MP

explanation.surface: A retired politician earns money as a chaperone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retirement' turns ANN into NNA, which 'charging' puts in DUES.
explanation.definitionFit: A duenna is an older woman supervising girls in a Spanish family, a chaperone.

clue.text: Some sour "fun" he misrepresented as wit

indicators.note: misrepresented means presented wrongly, so the letters come out in a different order

explanation.surface: A man's sour attempt at fun is passed off as wit.
explanation.definitionFit: Being able to see and make jokes is a gift for comedy, i.e. wit.

clue.text: Came across hard drug

parts.note: to come across someone is to have met them
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Someone stumbled upon a dangerous narcotic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hard' looks part of the definition 'hard drug' but only gives H.
explanation.definitionFit: Meth is short for methamphetamine, a stimulant narcotic.

clue.text: Wretched, lumpen young described by dictionary as "available to work"

indicators.note: wretched means in a sorry, broken state, so the word lumpen is broken up
described in the sense of drawn around, so the dictionary letters encircle the next piece

parts.note: OED is the Oxford English Dictionary

explanation.surface: A snobbish dictionary definition sneers at idle working-class youths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wretched' gives UNEMPL. 'described by' looks like a link but is the container: drawn round, as a circle is described.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone jobless is free to take up employment, so the phrase is a wry gloss.

clue.text: Regularly spout spiteful gossip, reactionary and foul

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the word spout
reactionary hints at going backwards, so the gossip word is read in reverse

parts.note: dirt is scandalous, malicious gossip

explanation.surface: A right-wing paper routinely spouts nasty, malicious tittle-tattle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' takes P and U from spout; 'reactionary' turns DIRT into TRID.
explanation.definitionFit: Putrid means rotten and stinking, hence foul.

clue.text: Feeling resentful? Bully migrants!

indicators.note: to bully is to push around, so the letters of migrants are pushed into a new order

explanation.surface: A tabloid-style rallying cry urging hostility towards immigrants out of resentment.
explanation.definitionFit: Smarting means stung or aggrieved, feeling hurt or resentful.

clue.text: They'd like to see capital punishment applied to spongers

parts.words: They'd like to see capital punishment
parts.note: people who want the gallows brought back are, jokingly, hangers
something applied is put on

explanation.surface: Pro-death-penalty readers are scorned as parasites.
explanation.definitionFit: Hangers-on are freeloaders who attach themselves to others for gain, i.e. spongers.

clue.text: Font selection?

parts.note: not typefaces: a font is a baptismal basin, and one is chosen to sponsor the baby there

explanation.surface: Choosing a typeface.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Font' looks typographic but is the church font at a christening.
explanation.definitionFit: A child's sponsor at baptism is chosen to stand at the font.

clue.text: Tours streets — and wishes one hadn't?

definitions.meaning: in the French city of Tours the word for streets is the plural of rue
to regret something done is to wish one had not done it

explanation.surface: A visitor wanders around town and then regrets it.
explanation.walkthrough: Tours is the French city, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: French for streets, and an English verb meaning regrets.

clue.text: Old timer snubbing two setters?

indicators.note: two calls for the shortened dog to appear twice
a snub nose is short, so snubbing cuts the tail letter off

parts.note: a setter is a breed of gun dog

explanation.surface: An elderly person cold-shoulders a pair of crossword compilers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setters' looks like crossword compilers but means dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: A dodo is an extinct bird, and figuratively an old-fashioned fogey.

clue.text: Leave nameless Bond villain with sulky expression

indicators.note: nameless means without N, the abbreviation for name

parts.note: Dr No is the villain of the first James Bond film
a pout is a sulky face

explanation.surface: An anonymous Bond villain departs with a sulk.
explanation.definitionFit: To quit a course or society is to leave it.

clue.text: Funny stuff derived from coffee (substitute an 'e' for 'o')

indicators.note: substitute tells us to swap one bit of the word for another, as the bracket spells out

parts.note: chicory root is roasted and used as coffee or a coffee substitute
the words an and e are taken literally as letters

explanation.surface: Something odd is made from a coffee, with an instruction to swap a vowel.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'e' is not a single letter swap: the whole phrase "an 'e'" replaces the O.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicanery is trickery or deceptive dealing, so funny business.

clue.text: Underground facility is, for some Swiss, integral to nuclear research centre

indicators.note: integral to means forming part of, so these letters go inside the centre

parts.note: CERN is the European particle physics lab near Geneva
German-speaking Swiss say ist for is

explanation.surface: An underground site in Switzerland is key to physics research.
explanation.definitionFit: A cistern is a tank for storing water, often underground.

clue.text: Note changes in passionate female making return to former state

indicators.note: changes in tells us one note is swapped for another inside the word

parts.note: a tigress is a fierce or passionate woman

explanation.surface: A fiery woman changes her musical tune and reverts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' stands for both swapped notes: TI out and RE in.
explanation.definitionFit: To regress is to go back to an earlier condition.

clue.text: Tell fib about Argentinian tree

indicators.note: about means around, so the fib surrounds the Argentinian

parts.note: to lie is to tell a fib
Che Guevara was born in Argentina

explanation.surface: Someone lies about a tree from Argentina.
explanation.definitionFit: The lychee is a Chinese fruit tree; lichee is a variant spelling.

clue.text: Further detailed Mail's nasty tendency to make value judgments

indicators.note: de-tailed, with the tail letter removed

parts.note: more means further or additional

indicators.note: nasty suggests the letters are mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: The Daily Mail's unpleasant habit of preaching is described at length.
explanation.definitionFit: Moralism is the practice of moralizing, passing ethical judgment on others.

clue.text: Attacks conservative newspaper, boring bunch of Nazis

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so the first pieces sit inside the Nazi letters

parts.note: the SS was the Nazi paramilitary organization
rag is slang for a low-quality newspaper

explanation.surface: Someone lays into a dull right-wing paper as a Nazi mob.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' looks like 'dull' but is the insertion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrag is to manhandle or assault someone, especially by the neck.

clue.text: Bones from start of Common Era held in institution

indicators.note: held in means placed inside, so the first year sits within the institution

parts.note: RI is the Royal Institution
AD 1 is the first year of the Common Era

explanation.surface: Bones from early Christian times are kept in a museum.
explanation.definitionFit: The radius is a forearm bone; radii is its plural.

clue.text: Might contain live wire?

parts.note: might means power or strength
to house something is to contain it

explanation.surface: An electrical building may hold a cable carrying current.
explanation.walkthrough: 'live wire' reads as electrical cable but means an energetic person.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe a dynamic, energetic person; the question mark marks the wordplay on electricity.

clue.text: Consider Daily Mail leaders welcoming eviscerated Europe

indicators.note: welcoming means taking in, so the leaders surround the other piece
leaders are the first letters of the two words
eviscerated means gutted, so only the outside letters remain

explanation.surface: Think about the Mail's editorials taking a gutted Europe to task.
explanation.walkthrough: D and M enclose E and E, the ends of Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: To deem is to judge or regard something in a certain way.

clue.text: Glossy rubbish loved primarily by English right

parts.note: tat is cheap, worthless stuff

indicators.note: primarily means at first, so just the opening letter of loved

explanation.surface: A trashy glossy magazine adored mainly by the English right wing.
explanation.definitionFit: Tatler is a British society magazine, a glossy in publishing slang.

clue.text: Hard stuff derived from champagne is sensational!

indicators.note: derived from means drawn out of these words, with the letters sitting inside them

explanation.surface: Strong drink taken from champagne is a sensation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard stuff' looks like strong liquor, but it is a rock.
explanation.definitionFit: Gneiss is a hard banded metamorphic rock.
